newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Gencor eyes Cuban nickel, cobalt deposits.
newsitem.headline: Gencor eyes Cuban nickel, cobalt deposits.

text.p: South African mining house Gencor Ltd has in its sights on two large nickel and cobalt resources in Cuba, Jopie Coetzee, senior manager for Gencor's nickel division, said on Friday.

While still assessing the size of the deposits -- they have a possible 30-year mine life -- and the viability of developing them, Gencor is drawn to the resources as they would slot into the group's expanding nickel portfolio, Coetzee told Reuters.
"We are busy assessing this lot and it is just too early to start talking about numbers, but both of them are substantial. You would be talking of plus 30 years," he said.

"Nothing is firm or imminent. We are going through our motions of assessing these deposits. We are busy developing a portfolio of nickel interests so we certainly remain interested in both Colombia as well as Cuba," Coetzee added.
Gencor's priority for its nickel operation is securing Colombia's Cerro Matoso SA, the world's fourth largest nickel mine, he said.

The South African mining house owns 52.3 percent of Cerro Matoso through its Dutch subsidiary Billiton and hopes to capture the Colombian government's 47.7 percent stake when it becomes available through privatisation.
"The priority is Cerro Matoso, which is imminent, and it is going to happen over the next couple of months," Coetzee said.
Cerro Matoso's current nickel production is 65 million pounds from 53 million two years ago.
Gencor is also interested in completing an abandoned nickel processing plant in eastern Cuba which had the capacity to process 30,000 tonnes of nickel a year, Coetzee said.
The plant was deserted by a consortium of former Soviet bloc countries in the early 1990s and its capacity is the minimum believed to be commercially viable.
"Thirty-thousand tonnes per year is the minimum size that would make such a project viable," Coetzee said.
The plant is located near one nickel and cobalt deposit. The second deposit, San Felipe, is in Cuba's Camaguey province.
"As far as San Felipe is concerned it is really a greenfields exploration project. There is still a lot of geological work to be done," Coetzee said.
Both deposits are close to the surface and so offer low cost development.
